cultivar: Yunnan large-leaf ripe pu-erh, usually a fine or gong-ting grade, inside Xinhui tangerine (Citrus reticulata 'Chachiensis') peel
processing: A Xinhui tangerine is cut at the top, hollowed, stuffed with loose ripe pu-erh and dried whole, in the sun or in low ovens, until the peel is hard; small green summer fruit make xiaoqinggan, ripe red autumn fruit make dahonggan, and loose chenpi pieces are also simply mixed with tea.
harvest_season: Fruit picked from July to August for the small green tangerines and from October to December for the red ones; the tea inside is sold by its own production year.
appearance_dry: A hard, hollow, dried tangerine the size of a golf ball (green-brown for xiaoqinggan, orange-brown for dahonggan) with a plug cut in the top, packed with dark ripe leaf.
appearance_liquor: Clear red-brown with a bright orange edge and a visible film of citrus oil on the surface.
appearance_wet: Softened dark leaf spilling from a pale, pithy peel that smells strongly of tangerine oil.
taste_profile: Bright tangerine peel and citrus oil over sweet, earthy ripe pu-erh: a bittersweet zest, dates and cocoa underneath, a warming, slightly medicinal peel note and a long citrus-sweet finish.

brewing.notes: Rinse once, briefly, with boiling water. Either brew the whole small tangerine with a few holes poked in it (one fruit per 150–200 ml, longer steeps), or break it up and use pieces of peel with the tea for a stronger citrus note. The whole fruit can be re-brewed all day or simmered.

vintage_note: Sold by the year the fruit was made and, for the better products, by the age of the ripe tea inside and the Xinhui origin of the peel; the category exploded around 2015–2017 and most of what is on sale is 1–5 years old. Aged chenpi is prized in Chinese medicine and the peel is thought to improve for years, so 3–5-year-old xiaoqinggan and older dahonggan with a stated tea year are sold at a premium, while cheap versions use young, rough shu and oven-dried peel from outside Xinhui. The tangerine does not need a vintage year to be good, but the tea inside does; ask what shu it is and how old.
description:
Chen pi pu-erh is ripe pu-erh packed inside a hollowed, dried tangerine, a marriage of two Chinese foodstuffs with their own long histories: aged tangerine peel, chenpi, from Xinhui in Guangdong, which is a traditional medicine ingredient and a kitchen spice, and shu pu-erh from Yunnan. The small green version, xiaoqinggan, became one of the biggest tea fads in China in the mid-2010s and is now a standard gift.

The fruit is cut, scooped, stuffed with loose ripe tea and dried whole until the peel is hard; sun-drying is traditional and slow, oven-drying is cheaper and common. Small green summer tangerines give a sharper, more aromatic peel; the ripe red autumn fruit, dahonggan, is sweeter and larger. The citrus oils soak into the tea as it dries, and the two keep trading flavours for years.

In the cup you get tangerine peel and citrus oil over the sweet, earthy base of ripe tea: a bittersweet zest, dates and cocoa underneath, a warming peel note that reads as medicinal in the pleasant sense, and a long citrus-sweet finish. Brew the whole fruit with holes poked in it for an all-day pot, or break it up for a stronger, faster session; boiling water either way.

It is sold by the piece, in bags and gift boxes, and by the year of making, with Xinhui peel and a stated tea age as the marks of a serious product. The traps are cheap, fishy young shu hidden under the citrus and peel from anywhere oven-dried in a hurry; a good one smells of clean tangerine oil and sweet tea, not of damp or burnt orange. Raw-tea versions exist but are rare, and the tangerine is doing the work either way.

It is the pu-erh for people who think they do not like pu-erh, and an easy winter tea to keep by the kettle.
history:
Pu-erh packed inside citrus is an established form of the tea: leaf is bound into a ball inside the peel of a fruit, and the best known version, xiaoqinggan, uses small green tangerines stuffed with tea.

It joins two older foods, dried tangerine peel and ripe pu-erh, but little reliable detail is documented about who first combined them or when. Its present fame as a gift tea is recent, and the dates usually quoted for that boom come from the trade.
